concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of Parliamentary Privileges: Articles 105 and 194
key_dimensions: Article 105 for Parliament vs. Article 194 for State Legislatures — structural symmetry and differences
Role of Article 105(3) before and after the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 — shift from House of Commons benchmark to codified position
Distinction between privileges of the 'House as a whole' vs. 'individual members'
Why privileges are not defined exhaustively in the Constitution — deliberate legislative silence and its implications

concepts.name: Freedom of Speech in Parliament: Scope and Limits under Article 105(1) and 105(2)
key_dimensions: Absolute nature of parliamentary free speech — no court can question proceedings (non-justiciability)
Critical exception: Members are NOT protected from Parliamentary Committee proceedings reported outside the House without authorization
Distinction between Article 19(1)(a) free speech (for citizens) and Article 105(1) parliamentary free speech — which is broader and why
How defamation laws, sedition laws, and Official Secrets Act interact (or do NOT apply) to parliamentary speech

concepts.name: Privilege of Freedom from Arrest: Civil vs. Criminal Cases
key_dimensions: Freedom from arrest applies ONLY in civil cases — NOT in criminal cases or preventive detention (a frequent UPSC trap)
Duration of protection: 40 days before and after a session, plus during the session itself
Whether this privilege extends to witnesses summoned by the House
Distinction between arrest and detention — how preventive detention laws override this privilege

concepts.name: Breach of Privilege and Contempt of the House: Definitions and Differences
key_dimensions: Breach of privilege = violation of a specific codified privilege; Contempt = broader — any act that obstructs or brings the House into disrepute
Every breach of privilege is contempt, but NOT every contempt is a breach of privilege — critical distinction
Who can initiate breach of privilege proceedings — any member, with Speaker/Chairman's consent
Examples of contempt not amounting to breach of privilege: misrepresenting proceedings in media, defaming a member outside the House

concepts.name: Privilege Committee: Composition, Powers, and Procedure
key_dimensions: Composition: 15 members in Lok Sabha, 10 in Rajya Sabha — nominated by Speaker/Chairman
Role: investigative and recommendatory — final decision rests with the full House
Whether Privilege Committee decisions are subject to judicial review — the constitutional tension
Difference in procedure between Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha in handling privilege motions

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Parliamentary Privileges: The Searchlight Case and Beyond
key_dimensions: MSM Sharma vs. Sri Krishna Sinha (Searchlight Case, 1959) — established that courts CANNOT question what happens inside the House
Raja Ram Pal vs. Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007) — Supreme Court held that courts CAN review expulsion of members for proportionality
The tension between Article 105 (privileges) and Articles 14, 19, 21 (fundamental rights) — which prevails?
P.V. Narasimha Rao vs. State (JMM Bribery Case, 1998) — immunity for speech AND vote in the House, even if bribe was taken

concepts.name: JMM Bribery Case Ruling (1998) and Its Implications for Privilege vs. Anti-Corruption Law
key_dimensions: Five-judge bench ruling: MPs who accepted bribe and voted accordingly were IMMUNE under Article 105(2); those who took bribe but did NOT vote were NOT immune
The logical and ethical paradox this created — rewarding the act of corruption if completed
Impact on Prevention of Corruption Act applicability to MPs
The 2024 Supreme Court Constitution Bench overruling this judgment — unanimous 7-judge bench ruling that bribery for vote/speech is NOT protected

concepts.name: Expulsion of Members as a Parliamentary Privilege: Scope and Judicial Scrutiny
key_dimensions: Power to expel is an inherent privilege — not explicitly listed in the Constitution
Raja Ram Pal case (2007): Supreme Court upheld judicial review of expulsion on grounds of proportionality and procedural fairness
Distinction between expulsion (permanent, by House) vs. suspension (temporary, by Speaker/Chairman)
Whether expelled member loses right to contest by-election — constitutional position

concepts.name: Privilege of Publication of Parliamentary Proceedings: Section 361 IPC and Beyond
key_dimensions: Publication of 'substantially true' reports of parliamentary proceedings is protected — Section 361 IPC and Article 105(2)
Exception: Reports of proceedings held in 'secret sitting' (in camera) are NOT protected
Distinction: Official Hansard (protected) vs. media reporting (conditionally protected)
Tension with press freedom — when does reporting a parliamentary speech attract defamation liability outside the House?

concepts.name: Collective vs. Individual Parliamentary Privileges: Classification and Examples
key_dimensions: Collective privileges (belong to the House): right to publish/exclude strangers, regulate internal proceedings, punish for contempt, receive immediate information of arrest of members
Individual privileges (belong to members): freedom of speech, freedom from arrest (civil), exemption from jury duty, exemption from being a witness
Why collective privileges are considered more important than individual privileges — UPSC frequently tests this hierarchy
Whether privileges of members extend to 'parliamentary committees' meeting outside Parliament House

concepts.name: Parliamentary Privileges and Fundamental Rights: Constitutional Conflict and Resolution
key_dimensions: Do privileges override Fundamental Rights? — Article 105 vs. Articles 14, 19, 21
Searchlight Case position: privileges are constitutional rights themselves — not subordinate to Part III
Post-Kesavananda Bharati position: Basic Structure doctrine — can Parliament claim privilege to violate basic structure?
Specific tension: Article 21 (life and liberty) vs. power to punish for contempt — imprisonment by House order without judicial trial

concepts.name: Codification of Parliamentary Privileges: Arguments For and Against
key_dimensions: Pre-44th Amendment: Parliament had same privileges as House of Commons — a foreign benchmark
44th Amendment, 1978: Removed the House of Commons reference — but did NOT define privileges, creating a vacuum
First Press Commission and various committees have recommended codification — government's reluctance and reasons
International comparison: UK has the Parliamentary Standards Act; India's lack of codification as both strength and weakness

concepts.name: Privilege of Regulating Internal Proceedings: Article 122 and Non-Justiciability
key_dimensions: Article 122: Courts cannot inquire into proceedings of Parliament — scope and meaning of 'proceedings'
'Proceedings' includes debates, votes, committee reports tabled in House — but does it include Speaker's administrative decisions?
Distinction between 'procedural irregularity' (non-justiciable) and 'unconstitutional action' (justiciable) — a key UPSC trap
Sub-Committee on Salaries and Allowances vs. privilege proceedings — which falls under Article 122?

concepts.name: Speaker and Chairman's Role in Privilege Matters: Powers and Limitations
key_dimensions: Speaker/Chairman's consent is the first filter for admitting a privilege motion — discretionary and final at that stage
Speaker can suo motu refer matters to the Privilege Committee
Whether Speaker's decision on privilege motion admissibility is subject to judicial review — constitutional ambiguity
Role conflict: Speaker as presiding officer vs. Speaker as guardian of House privileges — cases where these clash

concepts.name: Parliamentary Privileges vs. Anti-Defection Law: Intersection and Conflict
key_dimensions: 10th Schedule (Anti-Defection) adjudication by Speaker — is this a 'proceeding in Parliament' protected by Article 105?
Kihoto Hollohan case (1993): Anti-defection proceedings are subject to judicial review AFTER final order — carves out exception to Article 122
Can a member claim privilege protection for a vote cast under party whip versus conscience vote?
Whether anti-defection law itself constitutes a limitation on parliamentary privilege of free speech/vote

concepts.name: Privileges of Parliamentary Committees: Extension Beyond Parliament House
key_dimensions: Privileges extend to committee proceedings held outside Parliament buildings if duly constituted
Witnesses before Parliamentary Committees enjoy limited privilege — protection for evidence given, but committee can punish for contempt
Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs) — whether same privilege standards apply as to standing committees
Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) — can they summon Ministers? Privilege implications of refusal

concepts.name: Contempt Powers of the House: Punishment Mechanisms and Due Process Concerns
key_dimensions: House can impose: reprimand, admonition, suspension, imprisonment — but imprisonment terminates at end of session (a key fact)
No appeal lies to any court against a punishment order of the House for contempt — constitutional validity of this position post-Raja Ram Pal
Whether the House must follow principles of natural justice before punishing — contrast with judicial contempt proceedings
Imprisonment by Parliament vs. imprisonment by judiciary — which takes precedence if concurrent?

concepts.name: Privileges in the Context of Sting Operations and Media Reporting of Parliament
key_dimensions: Cash-for-query scandal (2005) — Lok Sabha expelled 11 members; Rajya Sabha expelled 1; judicial review question arose
Whether sting operation footage shown inside the House constitutes a 'proceeding in Parliament' attracting privilege protection
Live broadcast of Parliament proceedings — does the broadcasting agency enjoy privilege protection for technical errors?
Social media posts by MPs reproducing or misrepresenting parliamentary proceedings — does privilege cover this?

concepts.name: State Legislature Privileges under Article 194: Similarities, Differences, and State-Specific Issues
key_dimensions: Article 194 mirrors Article 105 — but state legislatures historically claimed powers beyond their actual privileges
Searchlight Case originated from Bihar Assembly — set the federal precedent
Whether a state legislature can punish a High Court judge for contempt — constitutional limits tested in multiple cases
MSM Sharma principle: State legislature privileges cannot override freedom of press guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) when the report is substantially true

concepts.name: Parliamentary Privilege and the Right to Information (RTI): Conflict Zone
key_dimensions: RTI Act 2005: Parliament and state legislatures are 'public authorities' — but Section 8 exemptions apply to sensitive information
Whether internal parliamentary proceedings, committee deliberations, and privilege committee reports are accessible under RTI
Speaker's office and Secretariat — RTI applicability vs. privilege protection of related documents
Central Information Commission (CIC) rulings on parliamentary records vs. Speaker's position on non-disclosure — ongoing tension
